articles.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
articles.summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation
articles.content:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

es.summary: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”

Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”

Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: CrowdStrike in Talks to Acquire Zscaler in One of the Biggest Cybersecurity Deals Ever
articles.summary: CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler in a deal that could rank among the largest in cybersecurity history. Bloomberg first reported the discussions on Friday, November 20, citing two people familiar with the matter who said talks were ongoing.
articles.content:
CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler in a deal that could rank among the largest in cybersecurity history. Bloomberg first reported the discussions on Friday, November 20, citing two people familiar with the matter who said talks were ongoing.

The discussions could still end without an agreement. Neither company has announced a deal or disclosed a proposed purchase price.

Zscaler shares jumped 18% in extended trading Friday, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. CrowdStrike declined to comment, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request.

At Friday’s regular close, Zscaler was worth about $32 billion. That figure reflects the stock market’s valuation, not what CrowdStrike has offered or might ultimately pay.

## Zscaler Would Add to CrowdStrike Falcon

CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform helps security teams detect and stop threats on laptops, servers, and cloud workloads. Zscaler controls how users and devices connect to applications and the internet.

Its Zero Trust Exchange checks identity and other signs of risk before allowing access. The two products address different parts of the same problem: Falcon can spot suspicious activity, while Zscaler can limit what a user or device can reach.

The companies already work together. A day before the takeover reports, CrowdStrike previewed an integration that lets Falcon share changes in user risk with Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine through open standards.

For example, if Falcon flags a user as risky after sign-in, Zscaler can use that signal to tighten access without waiting for the user to log in again. That work builds on a partnership expansion announced in September and is separate from the reported acquisition talks.

CrowdStrike’s earlier agreement to buy SGNL also focused on changing access as risk changes, rather than letting permissions stand until someone removes them.

Buying Zscaler would go further by bringing a cloud service that manages access to private applications and the public internet under the same owner as Falcon. The companies have not announced any plans to combine products or change customer contracts.

The talks come as major vendors buy tools that extend their reach beyond their main products. Google closed its $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in March 2026, adding cloud security tools to Google Cloud. Palo Alto Networks completed its $25 billion purchase of CyberArk earlier this year, expanding into tools that protect accounts with powerful system permissions.

Both are completed deals. Zscaler’s market value shows why the CrowdStrike talks matter, but it cannot yet be used to rank the proposed purchase.

For security teams, the practical question is whether common ownership would make it easier to investigate an alert and restrict access without switching tools.

Teams that use only one of the products would also want to know whether existing links to other vendors would remain supported and whether pricing would change.

For now, the existing partnership shows how the products can work together. It does not tell customers how a combined company would sell or support them.

articles.title: Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers Delivering Malware
articles.summary: A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers.
articles.content:
A malware campaign called CyberLeek is using more than 355 domains and subdomains to promote fake Grand Theft Auto VI PC launchers.

The sites offer what they claim is a leaked or early Windows release of GTA 6. Instead of a playable game, the download delivers a ZIP archive containing a malicious program disguised as an installer.

The campaign takes advantage of a familiar search: players looking for a GTA 6 PC release before they can get one through an official store.

Earlier reporting on fake GTA 6 downloads documented a separate operation that bundled password stealers, remote-access malware and file-destroying code with a fake game installer. Those findings do not establish what CyberLeek’s launcher does after it runs.

Researchers at the Vecert Foundation identified the malware distribution network and traced its activity to mid-October 2026, with notable spikes in November.

The count comes from domain and certificate records. It reflects the size of the infrastructure the researchers linked to CyberLeek, not the number of people infected or the number of distinct malware samples.

## Hackers Use 355 Domains to Spread Fake GTA 6 PC Launchers

One site examined by researchers advertised a playable GTA 6 port for Windows 10 and 11. It used search-friendly text and page markup that presented the supposed launcher as a software download.

A prominent button promised a direct file with “no ad wall,” making the page look like a convenient alternative to the pop-ups and redirects users might expect from an unofficial download site.

The download button did not always lead to the same file location. Researchers found that the page could send visitors to changing links on public hosting platforms, with a local ZIP archive available as a fallback.

That distinction matters for defenders: blocking one download URL may leave the original landing page reachable and other download paths available.

CyberLeek also used multiple domain endings and subdomains while keeping the same branding. This gave the campaign several places to send visitors if a site was blocked.

The approach echoes gaming search poisoning campaigns that use credible-looking pages to reach people searching for game tools or popular software. A high search ranking does not verify who published a file or what it contains.

The reported infection step is running the program inside the archive. Visiting the page or finding the ZIP in a Downloads folder does not, on its own, show that the installer ran.

In a separate case involving a fake GTA 6 demo, analysts identified Vidar, a program that steals passwords and browser sessions. Vecert did not name a specific malware family for CyberLeek or confirm what data the fake launcher collected.

Security teams can search DNS and web proxy logs for the reported hosts, then compare any matches with endpoint records for archive downloads and installer launches.

A generic script name or installer filename is not enough to establish a compromise. A recorded launch after a visit to a reported domain gives responders a stronger lead and a reason to check the device for unusual processes and network connections.

Players who downloaded the ZIP but did not run it should delete it without opening the installer. Anyone who ran the program should disconnect the device from the network and have it checked.

Since password and session theft can put accounts at risk even after the download is removed, use a clean device to change important passwords and revoke active sessions if compromise is suspected.

For future releases, check the publisher’s official channels or a trusted storefront rather than a site promising an early build.

articles.title: Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool for Spying on Government Networks
articles.summary: Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer
articles.content:
Hackers have rebuilt the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge to keep a quiet route into compromised networks. The modified Windows program, branded internally as NtMonitor VPN, can link an external network to a victim’s local network while leaving fewer of the traces defenders expect from a standard SoftEther installation.

Researchers link the tool to Webworm, a China-aligned espionage group with a history of targeting government organizations, particularly in Europe.

The distinction is that the bridge helps operators stay connected after a breach; the report does not show how they broke in. Nor does it name agencies newly affected by this build or establish what data, if any, was taken through it.

Earlier coverage of Webworm’s GraphWorm documented a separate backdoor that used Microsoft OneDrive for communications. NtMonitor serves a different purpose: it gives operators a network route rather than a built-in command shell.

Researchers from Rapid7 identified the modified VPN tool and attributed it to Webworm with moderate confidence in a November 19 report.

They compared a public 64-bit Windows sample with the matching SoftEther source release, version 4.44, build 9807, and found no added command-execution backdoor.

At the time of analysis, only one antivirus vendor on VirusTotal flagged the sample, even though it had been publicly available since January.

## Hackers Turn Legitimate VPN Software Into a Stealthy Tool

A VPN bridge connects networks rather than simply giving one user remote access. Every configuration Rapid7 examined linked a remote network to the local one.

That can make the Windows host running the bridge a route to other systems on its network. The risk comes from an existing feature being used without authorization, not from a newly disclosed SoftEther vulnerability.

Earlier reporting on Flax Typhoon’s SoftEther use illustrates how another group used the same open-source project to retain access after a breach.

The public sample described itself as “Network Monitor Software” from “Network Systems Solutions Inc.” and listed netcapa.exe as its original filename.

The disguise was inconsistent: some internal strings used NtMonitor branding, but the service entry point still referenced SEVPNBRIDGE, and several registry paths retained the SoftEther Project name.

The build also packaged a normally separate resource archive inside the program and stored its settings in an encrypted file. Together, those changes meant an installation could look unfamiliar even to a team that knew what stock SoftEther leaves behind.

The network traffic changed, too. Rapid7 found web request paths that resembled routine update traffic and a different marker in the opening exchange between VPN peers.

That made signatures written for standard SoftEther traffic less useful. A separate case involving modified WireGuard also involved a rebuilt VPN tool, but that version ran embedded code. Rapid7 found no comparable execution feature in NtMonitor; the bridge itself was enough to maintain access.

## How Government Defenders Can Detect Unauthorized VPN Bridges

Rapid7 found that configurations not considered likely tests pointed to addresses in AS20473, a hosting network associated with The Constant Company and Vultr.

That overlap with past Webworm activity supported the attribution, but the network number alone is not evidence of compromise. ESET’s earlier Webworm research documented targeting in Belgium, Italy, Poland, Serbia, and Spain.

Those countries describe earlier activity, not a confirmed victim list for NtMonitor. For defenders, the best starting point is an inventory of approved VPN services, the hosts allowed to run them, and the remote networks they are supposed to reach.

Investigate unexpected Windows services, firewall rule changes, and connections to unapproved peers together. Earlier reporting on malware in isolated government networks illustrates why investigators should check which systems a compromised host could reach, not just identify the first machine that raised an alert.

If a bridge is unauthorized, preserve its executable, configuration, and connection logs before removing it so responders can reconstruct where it led.

articles.title: Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials From Infected Computers
articles.summary: A Russian-speaking cybercrime operation has been stealing logins for US banks, the IRS and Social Security from infected Windows PCs. The victims were ordinary people. Many used a password manager and multi-factor authentication (MFA), and it did not
articles.content:
A Russian-speaking cybercrime operation has been stealing logins for US banks, the IRS and Social Security from infected Windows PCs. The victims were ordinary people. Many used a password manager and multi-factor authentication (MFA), and it did not help.

The attackers did not break into any bank or government agency. They went after the victim’s own computer, where saved passwords, cookies and password vaults sit in one place.

At least 57 US victims had a bank or government login in the stolen data. At least 46 had an ID.me, Login.gov, IRS or Social Security account.

Researchers at Hunt.io found the operation through an exposed open directory on a server in the Netherlands. The folder held the attackers’ stolen data, scripts and logs, and it showed that 603 infected computers were reporting to the group’s servers.

## Hackers Steal US Bank, IRS and Social Security Login Credentials

The attackers began with a small Python file that runs quietly in the background on Windows. Hunt.io says it was delivered by phishing, though it did not give the exact lure.

Once it was running, the infected PC checked in with the attackers’ servers, and they sent more tools based on what the victim had stored.

The first target was the web browser. The attackers broke the encryption Chrome and Edge use to protect saved passwords. Their scripts carried built-in keys that unlocked the stolen browser files later, away from the victim’s PC.

Hunt.io counted at least 3,345 decrypted logins from 16 victims, along with 30 cookie databases. Cookies matter because they prove a user has already signed in.

When an attacker copies one, the website may treat the attacker as the real user. This is how session cookie theft leads to account takeovers even when MFA is turned on.

In this case the attackers replayed stolen Microsoft 365 cookies to get live access tokens without a password or MFA prompt.

Password managers did not stop them either. One victim lost an entire LastPass vault with 2,880 logins, including Chase, Wells Fargo, IRS.gov, Medicare and PayPal.

Criminals have long cracking weak master passwords offline in stolen vaults. Here the group instead decrypted the vault data straight from the victim’s browser files.

They also guessed the master passwords of two 1Password users and copied a KeePass database from a developer’s computer.

The stolen data pointed to major US banks. Chase appeared in 31 victims’ data, Capital One in 20, Citi in 17 and Wells Fargo in 15. The ID.me and Login.gov accounts are the most worrying part, because those services open the door to the IRS, Social Security and the VA.

## Wider Theft and the Attackers’ Hidden Setup

The group did not stop at banks. Hunt.io found 6,570 cryptocurrency records from 67 victims, covering 44 platforms such as Binance, Coinbase, MetaMask and Kraken.

The attackers also went after login tokens from 35 AI tools, including Claude, Codex and Gemini. These tokens can expose chat history, project files and API keys.

To keep access after a cleanup, the attackers installed legitimate remote-management tools, Level.io and ScreenConnect. Because these are real business products, they can slip past some security filters.

The setup was built to stay hidden. One server ran three control systems, named HavoX, Phantom53 and Kraken Bridge. Twelve Cloudflare Workers domains sat in front of them, so victim traffic looked like normal web traffic.

Hunt.io says the system handled more than 1.2 million check-in messages over about three weeks. This kind of theft often ends in resale. Stolen logs can show up in an AI-powered marketplace selling infected computers. Hunt.io did not report a sale in this case.

Its evidence of who is behind the operation is the Russian-language text in the attackers’ own files. It found that text across 249 scripts and logs.

Home users who think a PC may be infected should use a clean device to change passwords, starting with email and banking. They should also sign out of every active session. Passwords alone are not enough, because a stolen session can stay valid after a reset.

Security teams should watch for pythonw.exe running .pyw files from the AppData\Roaming folder, which is where these implants live.

They should also block the listed domains and IPs. Hunt.io also advises binding sessions to compliant devices, keeping token lifetimes short and treating AI tool login files like SSH keys.

## Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.title: CISA Warns Hackers Are Actively Exploiting Four Flaws in Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap
articles.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 18, 2026, after finding evidence that attackers were already exploiting them.
articles.content:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added four flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 18, 2026, after finding evidence that attackers were already exploiting them.

The entries cover Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis and Vanderbilt University’s Research Electronic Data Capture platform, better known as REDCap.

The four products serve different roles: network storage, access to AI models, legacy web services and research data collection. That makes this update relevant to more than one IT team.

A storage administrator may own the Synology fix, but finding Apache Axis may require asking application vendors whether they bundle the library. CISA’s listing confirms exploitation of each flaw, not that the same attackers used all four.

CISA noted evidence of active exploitation in its November 18 security alert, but the agency did not identify any malware in that notice.

Separate reporting has linked attacks against Synology storage to C3RB3R ransomware and documented cryptomining malware in a REDCap incident. Those are incident-specific findings, not evidence of a shared campaign.

## Flaws in Synology, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap

CVE-2024-10441 is an output-handling flaw in a Synology system service that can let a remote attacker run code without signing in or requiring a user to take action.

The original Synology vulnerability coverage lists fixed builds across several DSM branches, including 7.2.2-72806-1 and 7.2.1-69057-6. Those builds are historical patch thresholds; administrators should install the latest supported release for their device.

CVE-2026-40217 affects LiteLLM’s custom guardrail testing feature. Guardrails are rules that control what an AI application accepts or returns.

In this case, code meant to run inside a restricted test environment could escape those limits. The maintainers say the feature requires proxy administrator credentials in default configurations and recommend upgrading to version 1.83.11 or later.

Earlier coverage of other LiteLLM gateway flaws explains why teams should also review what credentials and connected services the gateway can reach.

CVE-2026-90436 affects Apache Axis 1.x, a discontinued Java library for SOAP web services. The flaw can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a vulnerable server.

Rapid7 observed exploitation in a Confluence Data Center environment, where the attacker used the application’s credentials to access its database.

Apache does not plan to ship a fixed Axis 1.x release. Organizations using software that bundles Axis should follow that product vendor’s guidance; for Confluence Data Center, that means upgrading to 9.2.28 or an unaffected 10.x release.

CVE-2026-90817 is a code injection flaw in REDCap that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on the server. Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash, an identifier associated with a survey.

That prerequisite does not make the issue harmless: teams running public surveys should confirm their REDCap version and prioritize the vendor’s remediation guidance. The survey hash is not a malware file hash or an indicator of compromise.

## Patch Deadlines and What Defenders Should Check

Federal civilian agencies face a November 21 deadline for Synology DSM, Apache Axis and REDCap, and a December 2 deadline for LiteLLM.

CISA’s directive also sets expectations for checking whether attackers compromised certain systems before they were patched.

Recent coverage of an exploited Check Point flaw illustrates why that distinction matters: an update can close the entry point, but it cannot tell administrators what happened before installation.

Start with internet-facing systems and confirm which versions are actually running. For storage appliances, review unexpected logins, new administrator accounts and unfamiliar scheduled tasks.

Earlier reporting on Synology NAS ransomware attacks also recommends removing direct internet access to DSM management and keeping independent offline or off-site backups.

Where Axis is embedded in another product, verify the fix against the host product’s version rather than assuming a separate Axis package will appear in inventory.

## Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.summary: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out
articles.content:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

Image: blog.report-uri.com.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

articles.title: The Gentlemen Ransomware Gang Allegedly Claims to Have Breached NVIDIA
articles.summary: The Gentlemen ransomware gang listed NVIDIA on its dark web leak site on November 18, 2026, but the post does not prove that the group broke into the chipmaker’s systems.
articles.content:
The Gentlemen ransomware gang listed NVIDIA on its dark web leak site on November 18, 2026, but the post does not prove that the group broke into the chipmaker’s systems.

The listing shows a countdown and references ransom talks, but includes no sample files. NVIDIA has not publicly confirmed a breach, and there is no verified evidence that the group stole data or encrypted company systems.

The screenshot shows NVIDIA’s logo, its NVDA stock ticker, and a revenue figure of $303 billion with no reporting period. It also shows the words “DATA INFO – SOON” and a reference to Tox, a messaging service.

The countdown reads 237 hours, 50 minutes and 39 seconds, or just under 10 days. It does not say what will happen when the timer reaches zero.

## NVIDIA Ransomware Listing

The company details in the post are not evidence of access to an internal network. The image does not show which systems the gang claims to have reached, what files it claims to hold, or when any intrusion may have occurred. Without that evidence, it is not clear whether the claim concerns NVIDIA’s own systems, a third party, or neither.

The Gentlemen emerged in 2025 and operates as a ransomware-as-a-service group, meaning affiliates use the group’s tools to carry out attacks. As Cyber Security News previously reported in its profile of The Gentlemen, the group uses double extortion: stealing data and threatening to publish it while also locking files. That history does not establish that either happened at NVIDIA.

Previous Cyber Security News coverage of the gang’s attacks cited a Sophos review of 15 incidents. In some cases, attackers disabled endpoint security tools and backup services before encrypting systems less than 24 hours after gaining access. Those findings describe past attacks, not the NVIDIA claim. The leak post offers no technical evidence that the same methods were used here.

Ransomware tracker Breach House indexed the NVIDIA listing on November 18 and marked its leak status as pending. Its record documents when the claim appeared, not whether the gang accessed NVIDIA’s systems.

The listing also follows NVIDIA’s November 12 announcement that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. No evidence links that leadership change to the ransomware claim.

A company disclosure or independently verified files could help establish whether data was taken and where it came from. Even a genuine sample would not, on its own, show how the data was obtained or whether ransomware ran on company systems. Until such evidence emerges, the countdown marks a deadline set by the gang, not proof of a breach.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake Shipment ZIP Files and DLL Side-Loading to Deploy PureLogs and PureRAT Malware
articles.summary: Hackers are using a shipment-themed ZIP archive to launch a Windows malware chain that combines a legitimate signed application, DLL side-loading, and hidden Python code.
articles.content:
Hackers are using a shipment-themed ZIP archive to launch a Windows malware chain that combines a legitimate signed application, DLL side-loading, and hidden Python code.

The attack disguises its components as shipping material, images, documents, and a browser updater before running a payload linked to PureLogs and PureRAT infrastructure.

The case shows why a trusted digital signature does not make an entire software package safe. Here, the genuine application acts as the starting point, while a malicious library beside it drives execution.

Similar business email malware campaigns have used delivery complaints and download lures to distribute these malware families, although the supplied findings do not establish a connection between those operations.

Researchers from Unit 42, Shazan Khaja and Muhammet Algan, documented the activity in research dated November 16, 2026. They observed the infection chain on October 21 after a user downloaded the shipment-themed archive.

Their findings trace execution from the extracted files to a decoded Windows payload communicating with infrastructure attributed to PureLogs and PureRAT campaigns.

## Hackers Use Fake Shipment ZIP Files and DLL Side-Loading

Inside the archive, attackers placed a legitimate, validly signed, 32-bit Kingsoft PDF executable renamed to match the shipment lure. A malicious DLL sat alongside it.

When the user launched the executable, Windows loaded that nearby library, handing control to attacker-supplied code without requiring changes to the signed program itself.

The sequence unfolded within seconds. Windows Explorer wrote the DLL to disk at 03:02:53 UTC, consistent with archive extraction. The renamed application started at 03:03:06 and loaded the malicious library roughly one second later.

Archive extraction for the next stage began at 03:03:09, showing how quickly execution followed the user’s action. This approach resembles other trusted application side-loading attacks in which genuine software loads a hostile neighboring library.

However, the Kingsoft executable’s signature and hash are not evidence of infection on their own. Investigators need to examine its location, loaded libraries, and child processes rather than treating every copy as malicious.

The DLL launched a command sequence that opened a decoy PDF while preparing the hidden payload. A signed WinRAR command-line program, disguised with an image extension, extracted a password-protected archive into the public user directory.

The extracted package contained a Python runtime renamed to resemble Microsoft’s Edge updater. Several internal filenames used Korean-language phrases about chicken deliveries and refrigerator stock, unrelated to the shipment story.

These strings help describe the package, but they do not establish the attackers’ identity or the victims’ location. The supplied research does not identify a threat actor or explain how the download link reached the user.

## Disguised Python Loader Decodes the Final Payload

The renamed Python interpreter executed a one-line command that read another apparent PDF as raw bytes. Instead of displaying a document, it applied a repeating XOR key to recover Python code and passed that result to exec().

The document extension therefore concealed an encoded script rather than readable shipment information. The recovered script used randomized names and arithmetic expressions involving XOR, shifts, and addition to obscure its contents.

It then decoded a large Base64 blob and applied another repeating XOR operation, producing a Windows Portable Executable file with an MZ header. These layers separated the visible lure from the final executable payload.

Earlier reporting on Python DLL side-loading techniques provides context for this combination of trusted software and script execution. In this case, the decoded payload contacted the infrastructure listed below over TLSv1 on port 443.

Unit 42’s findings associate that infrastructure with PureLogs and PureRAT campaigns, rather than independently proving that both families executed on the observed endpoint.

For defenders, the strongest leads are behavioral: a signed application running from Downloads and loading a neighboring DLL, followed by command-shell activity, disguised archive extraction, and Python execution from a public directory.

A Python command that decodes an apparent document and immediately executes its contents is another important investigation lead.

## Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

A Python command that decodes an apparent document and immediately executes its contents is another important investigation lead.

articles.title: EU Accuses Temu of Failing to Stop Illegal Products, Citing Weak Security and Moderation Controls
articles.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), citing weak product checks, poor content moderation, and ineffective penalties against sellers. Announced on November 17, 2026, the findings question wh
articles.content:
The European Commission has preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), citing weak product checks, poor content moderation, and ineffective penalties against sellers. Announced on November 17, 2026, the findings question whether the marketplace takes effective steps to stop illegal products from reaching European buyers.

The case concerns Article 35, which requires platforms to put concrete measures in place to reduce identified risks. These are preliminary findings, not a final ruling. Although the concerns involve platform security controls, the announcement does not describe a data breach, malware attack, or confirmed compromise of Temu’s systems.

Investigators found that Temu requests product test reports for only a very small share of listings. Even when sellers must submit these reports, the company often does not check them. This leaves a gap between collecting safety documents and confirming that goods actually meet European Union safety requirements.

## Temu Breaching Digital Services Act

Temu classifies toys, electronics, and cosmetics as high risk, but allegedly does not give them priority during physical inspections. The Commission also found that the company often failed to follow up on spot check results. Inspection levels did not increase as the number of product listings grew.

The findings show why risk controls must grow alongside online services. Related Cybersecurity News coverage of EU platform oversight explains how DSA supervision extends to major digital services. For Temu, the immediate question is whether its checks can identify unsafe goods, rather than simply process an expanding volume of listings.

According to the Commission, Temu’s moderation focuses mainly on listing information and compliance with its own terms, rather than product safety. Its system for comparing listings with previously flagged goods also gives insufficient attention to unsafe products. Separately, an approved corrective action plan requires Temu to examine moderation limits and possible seller manipulation.

Human review presents another weakness. The number of moderators has not kept pace with listing growth, the Commission said. Taken together, these findings describe gaps across document checks, listing comparisons, physical inspections, and staff review. A listing that meets website rules does not necessarily prove the product itself is safe.

The Commission also questioned penalties aimed at individual stores instead of the traders behind them. One trader can operate several stores, allowing sales to continue elsewhere after a closure. Investigators found that sellers could commit numerous serious violations, including failed product safety checks, before Temu suspended any of their stores.

Temu can inspect the investigation file and respond in writing. The European Board for Digital Services will also be consulted. If confirmed, the findings could bring corrective orders and a fine reaching 6% of worldwide annual turnover. This differs from the DMA framework covered in Cybersecurity News’ Google enforcement report.

The new case follows a €200 million fine in May 2026 over inadequate risk assessment. Approval of Temu’s October action plan addressed that earlier breach, not the latest findings.

articles.title: New OWASP Top 10 Exposes Hidden Security Weaknesses in Neocloud and AI Infrastructure
articles.summary: A new OWASP Incubator Project highlights an overlooked AI security gap: the servers, networks, and data centers supporting AI systems receive far less attention than models, apps, and agents.
articles.content:
A new OWASP Incubator Project highlights an overlooked AI security gap: the servers, networks, and data centers supporting AI systems receive far less attention than models, apps, and agents.

The OWASP Top 10 Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks tries to fix that. It gives neocloud providers, their customers, and AI data center operators one shared list of the biggest infrastructure risks.

AI data centers pack thousands of GPUs, fast network fabrics, remote management controllers, shared storage, and complex scheduling tools into one place.

Much of this gear came from high-performance computing, where users were trusted. Today, the same parts run commercial GPU clouds, where unrelated companies share the same hardware. A flaw once considered minor can now put many customers at risk.

Many security tools also cannot see this layer. They watch operating systems, apps, and normal networks. They often miss firmware, management ports, and the special links that join GPU nodes. If the base is compromised, nothing running on top can be trusted.

Michael Katchinskiy and Yakir Kadkoda of the security firm Lava lead the project. The team selected risks from security research, incident reports, published CVEs, vendor documents, and practitioner talks.

Each candidate was scored on likelihood, impact, and detectability. Reviewers came from companies and schools such as Dell, Nebius, Google, IBM, and the University of Basel.

## OWASP Top 10 Exposes Neocloud AI Risks

The project does not cover prompt injection or model abuse. Other frameworks, including the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and MITRE ATLAS, handle those.

OWASP ranks the risks from most to least severe. The first five are rated critical. These are hardware and firmware tampering, weak networks between GPUs, poor separation between tenants, unsafe out-of-band management, and supply chain compromise.

Lower on the list are weak facility systems, careless handling of data and model files, gaps in certifications and provider honesty, unsafe operations tools, and slow patching.

Firmware and management controllers deserve a close look. A baseboard management controller, or BMC, lets admins control a server even when its operating system is off. If a hacker takes it over, the access can survive a reinstall and follow the server to the next customer.

This is not just theory. Researchers recently found 36,872 internet-exposed IPMI interfaces, and about 67 percent leaked password-based authentication data before login.

Some belonged to GPU and bare-metal cloud providers. Earlier, a flaw in AMI MegaRAC software (CVE-2024-54085) let attackers skip login on affected servers.

Our own BMC firmware vulnerabilities report showed how weak Supermicro patches left the door open. Tenant isolation is another weak spot.

The NVIDIAScape container escape flaw, CVE-2025-23266, let a malicious container gain root access on a GPU host. It hit toolkit versions up to 1.17.7. That is the exact kind of problem the OWASP list warns about.

The framework notes that attackers have begun targeting AI infrastructure. It cites a TIME report about a US tech firm whose AI data center lost intellectual property.

It also cites a conviction for stealing AI data center designs and claims of a 10-petabyte theft from China’s Tianjin supercomputing center. The authors also warn that GPU shortages mean customers often pick whatever provider has capacity, not the most secure one.

articles.title: Australia’s Supermarket Chain Coles Investigates Cyber Security Incident
articles.summary: Australian supermarket chain Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, with outside experts helping secure its systems. The retailer disclosed the incident on November 16, 2026, and said stores and online shopping remain open. Investigators ha
articles.content:
Australian supermarket chain Coles is investigating a cybersecurity incident, with outside experts helping secure its systems. The retailer disclosed the incident on November 16, 2026, and said stores and online shopping remain open. Investigators have found no evidence that customer, employee or supplier data has been compromised or removed.

Coles is working with the Australian Cyber Security Center and global cyber security experts to contain the incident and protect its IT environment. The company said it would continue engaging with relevant agencies and regulators as its investigation develops, while closely monitoring systems for signs of further security problems.

The current finding is not a final guarantee that no data was affected. Coles qualified its statement as being based on its investigation so far. Its public update does not identify an attacker, explain how the incident began, name affected systems, or confirm whether ransomware was involved. Those details remain unknown.

Customers can continue using the Coles app and website normally. Flybuys accounts show no indication of impact, while Coles Plus, Coles Plus Delivery and QuiteLike subscriptions remain available. Gift cards also continue working. These updates distinguish the confirmed incident from claims of widespread service failure or account compromise.

## Coles Investigates Cyber Security Incident

However, Coles acknowledged that a small number of customers were experiencing problems with Liquorland click-and-collect orders. The retailer is investigating those issues but has not publicly explained their cause or confirmed a connection to the security incident. It currently says customers do not need to take any incident-specific action.

The official Coles incident update remains the main source for confirmed findings. Other retail incidents provide context, not evidence about this case. Cyber Security News previously covered retail chains facing cyberattacks, including Marks & Spencer, Harrods and Co-op. Their experiences should not be treated as proof of the methods used against Coles.

Separate reporting on the Harrods customer data breach shows why retailers must distinguish attacks on their own systems from incidents involving suppliers. Coles has not named a third-party provider as the source of this incident. No public technical findings currently support attributing it to a particular group, tool or entry method.

Coles warns customers to watch for unexpected emails, texts, calls and requests for personal details. It says unsolicited emails or SMS messages will never request passwords or sensitive account information. Customers should avoid suspicious links, use unique passwords, and verify doubtful messages.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

articles.title: Cursor Reveals How a Leaked Fireworks AI Key Led to a Backdoored Claude Code Extension
articles.summary: Cursor has traced its October security breach to an access key exposed by Fireworks AI. The attacker used that key to steal historical coding agent records, find more credentials, and eventually place backdoored Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s mar
articles.content:
Cursor has traced its October security breach to an access key exposed by Fireworks AI. The attacker used that key to steal historical coding agent records, find more credentials, and eventually place backdoored Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace cache. Its November 13 update connects the vendor exposure to the malicious packages discovered on October 29.

The stolen key, which Cursor had issued to Fireworks, provided read-only access to a shared storage bucket. It held limited coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions outside Privacy Mode that Cursor was permitted to use for model training. Some records contained credentials that had not been removed.

Cursor said fewer than 0.05% of users had coding agent traces exposed, while less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed. These figures describe different parts of the incident and should not be treated as the number of users who installed malware.

Using credentials found in those records, the attacker reached selected software services used by Cursor. The exposed information included archived, non-production source repositories, limited support records and emails, usage metrics, contact details, conversation summaries, and some credentials customers had sent to support.

On October 29, a credential stolen from exposed internal data allowed the attacker to place modified Claude Code packages directly into the cache serving Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. Cursor said Anthropic did not publish the packages, its product was not vulnerable, and Open VSX never hosted the malware. This corrects earlier reporting that placed the package on Open VSX.

## Claude Code Backdoor Worked

According to Cursor’s incident update, at most 5,000 users requesting specific cached versions potentially received malicious builds during roughly 11 hours. The affected packages were Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS. That is a potential distribution count, not confirmation of 5,000 successful backdoor connections.

Cyber Security News’ initial technical analysis described injected JavaScript that ran when the extension loaded, without requiring a Claude conversation. It collected host details, added an SSH key labeled svc-telemetry, and attempted a reverse SSH tunnel to 134[.]209[.]82[.]225. The initial data upload included environment variable names, not their values.

Its follow-up on Cursor’s confirmation detailed macOS LaunchAgent persistence and a Windows scheduled task with a Startup-folder fallback. Scripts retried connections about every 60 seconds. Cursor said coding errors and missing administrator rights blocked remote login on most hosts, but did not prevent other malicious changes or host data collection.

## Wider Fireworks AI Breach Impact

The Fireworks AI breach report covered broader exposure involving account and billing records, selected datasets, and incomplete model weights. Fireworks’ November security update also described access through a cloud provider hosting development machines. Those broader findings do not establish that every customer lost the same data.

Other customers reported separate impacts. Notion’s disclosure involved AI chat transcripts used by Insights across fewer than 1% of workspaces, without a breach of Notion’s systems. Uber’s disclosure concerned personal information, including driver’s license details, belonging to thousands of U.S. drivers. Neither disclosure establishes involvement in Cursor’s extension attack.

Cursor moved inference traffic away from Fireworks, revoked vendor access, rotated internal credentials, rebuilt the extension marketplace, and expanded secret scanning and network restrictions. It also redeployed production infrastructure as a precaution. The company believes the incident is contained and said the last observed attacker activity, on November 1, was blocked. Privacy Mode prompts, customer code repositories, and official Cursor updates were unaffected.

Affected developers should follow Cursor’s cleanup notice. Removing the extension alone may leave SSH keys and startup scripts behind. Cursor advises checking endpoint evidence, isolating affected machines, removing persistence, rotating accessible credentials from a trusted system, and assessing whether rebuilding is needed.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

Some records contained credentials that had not been removed.

Using credentials found in those records, the attacker reached selected software services used by Cursor. The exposed information included archived, non-production source repositories, limited support records and emails, usage metrics, contact details, conversation summaries, and some credentials customers had sent to support.

articles.title: CISA Warns of Check Point 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited to Gain Root Access
articles.summary: CISA has warned that attackers are exploiting a Check Point security flaw that lets a local user gain root access on affected appliances. The agency added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 13, 2026, confirming
articles.content:
CISA has warned that attackers are exploiting a Check Point security flaw that lets a local user gain root access on affected appliances. The agency added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 13, 2026, confirming that the vulnerability is being used in real attacks.

Check Point said it observed exploitation against “a couple of dozen customers.” The flaw carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and affects the DynamicCLI service in Gaia OS. Successful exploitation allows commands to run with the highest operating system rights, putting affected firewalls and management systems at risk.

## Check Point Root Access Vulnerability

The weakness sits in dynamic_server, a process that runs as root and handles extended command-line functions. It receives requests through /tmp/dynamic_socket, a local communication socket. On vulnerable systems, this socket has permissions set to 0777, allowing any local user to write to it without proper access restrictions.

The service also fails to authenticate the process sending a request. It executes the received command as root, turning limited local access into full system control. However, this is not a standalone remote code execution flaw. An attacker must already have local code execution on the appliance before exploiting it.

Cybersecurity News previously covered Check Point firewall attacks involving PHP2Shell, where attackers used this privilege escalation flaw after gaining initial access. That distinction matters because fixing an entry point alone does not remove every weakness attackers could use after reaching a device or gaining a service account.

## Affected Products and Available Fixes

According to Check Point’s security advisory, affected products include Force Firewalls, Management and Log Servers, Multi-Domain management and logging systems, and Maestro Orchestrator. Vulnerable releases span R81, R81.10, R81.20, R82, R82.10, and R82.20. Check Point Spark Firewalls and Smart-1 Cloud are not affected by this flaw.

Check Point has released fixes in Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator updates. Protected releases start at R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132, and R81.20 Take 174. The correction blocks and logs unauthorized DynamicCLI requests. R81 and R81.10 are listed as end-of-support versions in the advisory.

For temporary mitigation, administrators can stop the service and prevent its restart by running dbset process:dynamic_server, followed by dbset :save. Check Point warns that this disables the Dynamic CLI commands described in its documentation. Administrators should account for that operational impact rather than treating the workaround as a permanent replacement for patching.

The daemon records received commands in /var/log/dynamicCli.log. Requests that lack the expected Clish wrapper need investigation. Check Point also recommends checking for unusual commands involving account creation, SSH keys, downloads, or sensitive files. After patching, /tmp/dynamic_socket should show permissions of 0660, owned by root and the config group, rather than 0777.

Earlier Check Point VPN zero-day coverage showed how gateway flaws can expose sensitive information. This case requires local access, but confirmed exploitation makes patching and compromise checks urgent. CISA’s alert urges organizations to prioritize known exploited vulnerabilities.

articles.title: FBI Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Gain Privileged Access in Under Three Hours
articles.summary: The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours.
articles.content:
The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Its November 13, 2026, FLASH alert describes how attackers combine stolen credentials, exposed applications, and cloud permissions to shorten the gap between discovery and compromise.

ARTEX is an open-source security testing framework, not a malware family. Written in Go, it connects external large language models to agents that turn instructions into commands.

Operators set objectives while agents scan targets, run tools, review results, and adjust failed steps with limited human input throughout an attack campaign.

## ARTEX Accelerates Enterprise Attacks

As covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s ARTEX enterprise attack analysis, the framework links familiar weaknesses rather than relying on a single new exploit. Agents can investigate cloud permissions, map Active Directory, and test access paths. Google observed individual automated bursts lasting two to 25 seconds, leaving defenders little time to assess connected events.

The FBI lists attacks involving SQL injection, missing API authentication, exposed passwords, and abuse of trusted cloud connections. After entry, agents have added credentials to existing applications, deployed web shells, and attempted credential theft. Other activity included searching for Windows systems without endpoint protection and mapping over 110,000 directory objects.

Microsoft previously linked ARTEX to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group targeting Microsoft 365 environments through compromised ConnectWise application credentials.

Attackers attempted access to more than 2,250 tenants using permissions customers had already approved. That number measures targeting, not confirmed breaches, and successful sign-ins alone do not establish customer data theft.

The FBI advisory brings these findings together, warning that ARTEX also targets overlooked supplier portals, sales tools, and mobile backends. Its under-three-hour figure describes some observed intrusions, not a fixed capability. Publicly exposed consoles exceeded 1,600 by early November, although exposed installations do not automatically prove malicious use by their operators.

A separate WorkOS breach report shows the risk to internal business applications. WorkOS detected unauthorized access to a sales application containing customer contact details and conversation records, including Slack excerpts. Its CEO identified ARTEX involvement, while the company reported no evidence that production services or WorkOS application data were affected.

Another Microsoft investigation documented ARTEX agents searching GitHub for exposed secrets. In one case, an agent progressed from repository searches to stealing Azure Key Vault data within five minutes.
